title: Three expressions (CCC 2700–2724)

segments.voice: Yesterday, guides for prayer: families, ministers, religious, prayer groups, directors. Your line was nobody learns alone. Whose answer did you listen to? Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

Noon, in a quiet church, three people in the same pew. The first is murmuring the words of a prayer under her breath, lips moving, beads sliding through her fingers. The second has a small Bible open on his knee and keeps reading one line, then looking up, then reading it again. The third isn't doing anything anyone could see. No book, no words. Just sitting, eyes resting on the tabernacle at the front. From the back of the church they might look like three different things. The Catechism says they're three ways of doing one thing. Today: three expressions.
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, ONE PEW.` → `WORDS, A BOOK, NOTHING VISIBLE.` → `ONE THING, THREE WAYS.`

segments.voice: First, vocal prayer: prayer with words, said aloud or under the breath. The Catechism points out that Jesus himself taught a prayer with words. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thus therefore shall you pray: Our Father who art in heaven." We're bodies as well as spirits, it says, so it's natural for prayer to come out through the lips. But the words are meant to carry the heart with them, not replace it. That's the voice. Second, meditation. This is the mind at work: a search, the Catechism calls it, trying to understand what God is asking. It usually leans on something: a page of scripture, an icon, a prayer of the liturgy, the writings of the saints. It names lectio divina, slow holy reading, and the rosary. The model is Mary after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Thought, imagination, feeling and desire all get used. That's the mind. Third, contemplation. Here the Catechism quotes Teresa of Avila, who described it as close sharing between friends, taking time to be alone with the one who loves us. And it tells a story from the French village of Ars. A peasant there used to pray before the tabernacle, and the words he said about it were simple: I look at him, and he looks at me. The Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus. That's the gaze. Three expressions, one prayer. The same person might use all three in a single afternoon.
screen: `VOCAL PRAYER: THE VOICE.` · `MEDITATION: THE MIND.` · `CONTEMPLATION: THE GAZE.` · `THREE EXPRESSIONS, ONE PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try all three, briefly. Settle, and breathe. Voice: if you pray, say one line of a prayer you know, slowly, out loud or in a whisper. If you don't, say one line of something that matters to you. Mind: take one word from that line and turn it over. What does it ask of you today? Gaze: then let the words go, and just rest your attention, the way the peasant of Ars did. Look, and let yourself be looked at. The bell holds the time.
Three expressions. In the Catechism: vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation, prayer with the voice, with the mind, and with the gaze. Today's words.
Your line: voice, mind, gaze. Today, notice which of the three comes naturally to you, and give the other two one honest minute somewhere in the day. Day one thousand one hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics pray vocally with the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the prayers of the Mass; meditate through lectio divina and the mysteries of the rosary; and some practice silent contemplation, often in adoration before the Blessed Sacrament.

fork.setup: a peasant of Ars prays before the tabernacle. how does he describe what he does there?
options: he recites every prayer he knows.
he looks at him, and he looks at me.
he asks for a good harvest.
fork.reveal: in his telling, it is looking, and being looked at. the Catechism calls contemplation a gaze of faith.

original.note: Latin: contemplation — the word the Western Church used for the third expression, the quiet gaze of prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: real prayer means saying the right words.
what it means: the Catechism names three expressions: vocal prayer, meditation and contemplation, the voice, the mind and the gaze.
what a scholar hears: the section quotes Teresa of Avila's definition of mental prayer and the peasant of Ars, and calls contemplation a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus.
